event.active_new_world_frontier_b_01_iro: You pay 2,000 Berrys to release the papers and end the dispute immediately.
Pay the disputed penalty
The broker calls your bluff and adds a 1,000-Berry handling charge.
He calls the scale master himself and releases the papers before the review is finished.
He refuses the accusation but agrees to reopen the scale records.
He admits the discrepancy may be internal and suspends the penalty.
Pressure the broker
You combine two shipment numbers and hand the broker a stronger case for the penalty.
You match every seal and prove exactly where the missing tonnage was diverted.
The paperwork stays contradictory and the broker keeps the cargo papers.
You find a four-ton transfer recorded at the wrong berth.
Rebuild the manifest
A freight contract promises payment for forty tons, but the yard scale records thirty-six after unloading. The broker blames the crew and demands a penalty before releasing the cargo papers.
The Missing Tonnage
The broker records your name for the next available berth, a promise that exists only in this contract’s history.
Take future berth priority
The yard posts the corrected tonnage where the waiting crews can see it.
Demand a public correction
The broker pays the refund and closes the contract without further noise.
Take 1,500 Berrys
A scale-master’s note confirms the missing load was shifted inside the yard. The broker offers a quiet refund, a public correction, or priority on a future berth.
The Scale Master’s Note
You collide with a fleeing worker and both of you go down under falling tools.
You clear the staging and kick the loose tool chest out of the impact zone.
You clear most workers, but one bench and its tools are lost.
You get the last workers off the staging before the rudder swings through.
Clear the staging
The rope burns through your hands and the rudder slams into the staging.
You arrest the swing completely and give the crane crew a clean recovery angle.
You slow the swing but cannot stop the rudder from crushing a workbench.
You hold the rudder off the workers until the crane crew secures a second line.
Hold the guide rope
You stay clear and direct attention to the failing hook while trained workers handle the load.
Warn the crane crew
A lifting chain snaps above a crowded drydock and a suspended rudder drops crooked. Workers scatter while the foreman shouts that one support hook is still holding.
The Drydock Chain Snaps
You put 2,000 Berrys toward the stopped workers’ wages and the inspection continues without a walkout.
Cover one lost shift
The crew replaces only the broken chain and returns to work under uneasy looks.
Let the yard resume
The foreman closes the lift until every chain is inspected, costing the yard time but preventing another drop.
Back the workers’ stoppage
The rudder is finally grounded, but the foreman wants the line reopened immediately. Several workers point at a second chain with the same cracked links.
The Yard Stops
You spend 1,250 Berrys on fresh stock and the workshop discards the questionable batch.
Buy fresh rivets
You take a place on the hammer line and help finish the plate before the berth closes.
Join the hammer line
The plate finishes late, but the crew works without forcing overheated metal.
Slow the furnace
Your shipwright reorganizes the work sequence and gets the plate seated without overheating it.
Put your shipwright on the plate
A workshop falls behind on a hull plate while a furnace runs too hot. The master needs either extra hands, a slower safe pace, or money to buy a fresh batch of rivets.
The Red Rivet Shift
The inspector bolts on a quick reinforcement that buys some margin without a full repair.
Take the quick plate
You leave the seam unchanged and clear the berth before closing.
Decline the work
The yard braces the seam properly and hands the ship back in stronger condition.
Pay for reinforcement
Your shipwright uses the remaining berth time to reinforce the seam with the crew’s own labor.
Let your shipwright patch it
A yard inspector points out a vulnerable seam on your ship after a crane wake slams vessels against the quay. The berth closes soon, so any reinforcement must be chosen now.
The Harbor Reinforcement Offer
You read an outdated column and accuse the wrong clerk, losing leverage immediately.
You reconstruct the whole pattern and identify every displaced crew before the list can be changed.
The board shows irregular changes, but none clearly prove who made them.
You find three handwritten swaps that match cash payments in the margin.
Audit the queue board
The clerk flips the accusation onto you and the queue turns into a shouting match.
The whole rail backs you, and a yard supervisor arrives before the clerk can alter the list.
The clerk denies everything and nobody wants to lose their own place by backing you.
Two captains confirm the offer and force the clerk to reopen the queue ledger.
Expose the offer publicly
You leave the clerk and waiting captains to settle the queue without you.
Ignore the offer
A dock clerk quietly offers to move a damaged merchant ship ahead of three smaller crews for cash. The waiting captains can hear every word from the rail.
A Place in the Repair Queue
The supervisor rebuilds the queue around immediate seaworthiness instead of payment or arrival time.
Prioritize dangerous damage
The displaced crews regain their places, even though the yard loses hours reorganizing berths.
Restore the original order
You hand the problem back once the false swaps are removed.
Leave policy to the yard
The supervisor takes the queue ledger and asks how to handle the crews already displaced. Restoring every berth will delay several urgent repairs.
The Queue Ledger
event.active_new_world_frontier_b_01_sph: You follow a washed-out marker and circle back toward the coast.
You find a forgotten shortcut that reaches the farm before the first hard rain.
You find the old trail but lose time in a collapsed gully.
You identify the inland trail and avoid the exposed cliff entirely.
Find the old inland trail
You bring the injured runner safely home, but the farm must wait for another courier.
Carry the runner back
A wet ledge gives way and you slam against the rock, losing precious minutes.
You reach the farm dry and early enough for the medicine to be prepared immediately.
You crawl through the worst section, but the storm catches you before the farm.
You cross the exposed ledges before the rain becomes dangerous.
Take the cliff path
A runner twists an ankle halfway to an isolated farm. The medicine in their satchel must reach a feverish elder before the coastal rain turns the cliff path into mud.
Medicine Above the Cliffs
You sleep under a leaking awning while the elder rests beside the medicine.
Give the dry room to the patient
You leave immediately and accept a miserable return walk to keep moving.
Head back in the rain
The family crowds everyone together until the storm passes.
Share the room
The medicine reaches the farm as heavy rain closes the path behind you. The family can spare only one dry room and asks whether you will stay or leave it to the patient.
Rain at the Farm
Your words sound like favoritism; both families turn on you and the healer.
You get both households to accept a shared plan before the healer even asks.
Nobody leaves, but the shouting continues while the child worsens.
Both families stop shouting long enough to hear the healer’s decision.
Calm both families
You step aside and let the healer carry the whole decision alone.
Leave it to the healer
You misread the worst signs; the room erupts and the healer loses precious time.
You spot a dangerous complication early and give the healer a clear order of urgency.
The symptoms overlap too much to settle the dispute cleanly.
You identify which child is in immediate danger and the room quiets enough to decide.
Compare the symptoms
Your medic confirms the more urgent case and gives the healer a second professional voice.
Ask your medic to assess
A village healer has one fever vial left while two families arrive at once. One child is already shaking, and both households insist they were promised the medicine.
The Last Fever Vial
You leave 1,500 Berrys for the next medical shipment and the healer records the debt as paid.
Fund the next stock
The sickest child receives the full treatment; the other family must wait for the next supply boat.
Use the full dose
The healer divides the medicine and watches both children through the night with uncertain results.
Split the vial
The shouting has stopped. The healer uncorks the vial and asks whether the village should spend everything now or divide the dose and accept the risk.
Who Gets It
You spend 750 Berrys on cord so the families can start a second repair.
Buy fresh cord
You leave the families to settle tomorrow’s catch among themselves.
Refuse to choose a boat
You spend the afternoon helping reinforce the shared net before the tide turns.
Mend the weakest sections
Your shipwright shows the fishers a faster splice and gets a second net usable by sunset.
Put your shipwright on it
Three fishing families spread one usable net across the beach. Each boat needs it at dawn, but there is not enough cord left to repair the other two.
One Net for Three Boats
You cover 2,000 Berrys for medicine so the entire catch can feed the village.
Pay for the clinic yourself
Every household receives food tonight, but no money is set aside for the clinic.
Divide it by household
The village keeps less food but sets aside money for the next medical purchase.
Sell a portion for medicine
You step away before the catch is divided and let the fishers settle it.
Leave the argument alone
A small boat returns with a rare heavy catch after several empty days. Before the fish are unloaded, hungry households argue over whether to divide them or sell enough for medicine.
The Shared Catch
A loose block rolls over your leg and the breach widens before anyone can reset it.
You lock two fallen slabs together and turn the worst current away from the houses.
You hold one slab briefly, but the current forces everyone back.
You wedge the largest slab long enough for villagers to pack smaller stones behind it.
Brace the broken wall
You help the youngest villagers reach high ground while others fight the breach.
Carry children uphill
You slip in the wash and hit a doorpost while one family abandons its supplies.
You clear all three houses and save the dry food stored under the rafters.
You reach one house, but the second is already ankle-deep in water.
You get the nearest families outside before the water reaches their sleeping mats.
Race the flood to the houses
A section of Sphinx’s rough stone tidewall collapses as the sea rises. Water pours toward three low houses while villagers drag baskets and children uphill.
The Tidewall Gives Way
The houses empty slowly enough for families to recover blankets and tools.
Join the bucket line
You sit out the last minutes of the emergency and keep the injury from worsening.
Stop and bind your wounds
You move the driest sacks uphill before seawater ruins the village’s reserve.
Save the grain sacks
The first rush is contained, but the flooded houses keep filling from below. Someone shouts for a bucket line while another group tries to save sacks of grain.
The Bucket Line
event.active_new_world_frontier_b_01_sto: The yard seals the worst seam quickly and sends you away before the berth dispute begins.
Take the cheap patch
You keep your Berrys and clear the alley before the rival crew arrives.
Leave before paying
You pay 2,500 Berrys and the yard completes a solid repair before the rival crew arrives.
Pay the rush fee
Your shipwright rejects the worst shortcuts and turns the patch into a dependable repair.
Have your shipwright supervise
A back-alley yard offers to patch your ship before nightfall, no questions asked. The foreman wants cash up front and warns that a rival crew may claim the berth.
The Black-Sail Repair Yard
You trust a rehearsed detail and hand leverage to the more dangerous crew.
You expose a planted lie and make the false claim collapse in front of the dock.
Both stories contain enough truth to keep the standoff alive.
You catch a detail only the real owner could know about the crate’s bindings.
Read the two stories
You make it clear the box is not yours and leave the two crews to settle their claim.
Step away from the crate
Your warning is taken as a challenge and someone smashes you into the crate.
The dock turns against anyone who starts violence, and both crews accept a neutral check.
The weapons lower, but neither crew agrees to leave without a ruling.
You force both crews to name terms instead of reaching for weapons.
Talk both crews down
A dock porter drops an unmarked black crate beside your baggage, then vanishes into the crowd. Two armed crews immediately arrive, each claiming the box belongs to them.
The Wrong Black Crate
You settle the ownership and walk away before learning what the crate contains.
Refuse the money
You refuse to arbitrate contraband and force both crews to clear the table elsewhere.
Make both crews leave
You accept 1,500 Berrys and make the owner remove the crate from the dock immediately.
Take the settlement fee
A tavern keeper drags out a scarred table and demands the crate be settled there, not with blades. The real owner offers a fee if you finish the dispute.
The Claims Table
You stay under the cliff but keep enough eyes on the mooring lines that nobody approaches unnoticed.
Keep the berth and double watch
You keep the cheap sheltered berth and trust that the warning was meant for someone else.
Ignore the warning
You pay 1,000 Berrys for a noisier public berth and leave the sheltered cliff before dark.
Move to the open quay
Your navigator identifies a safer anchor angle that makes a cut line less likely to send the ship onto rocks.
Ask your navigator to inspect currents
A scarred fisher quietly warns that ships moored under the eastern cliff are cut loose after midnight. Your berth is cheap, sheltered, and exactly where they are pointing.
The Quiet Anchorage Warning
They surround you, take 1,000 Berrys by force, and send you through under jeers.
The watchmen lose the crowd completely and abandon the lane before a fight starts.
They lower the price but keep the lane blocked for everyone else.
The waiting carriers refuse to pay once someone openly challenges the watchmen.
Call their bluff
You hand over 750 Berrys and move through while the watchmen keep collecting behind you.
Pay and pass
You point to a real mark by mistake and give the watchmen room to mock the accusation.
You expose every stamp as recycled fraud and the whole queue refuses to pay.
You prove the stamps are inconsistent, but the men still control the lane.
You identify copied marks from unrelated docks and turn the waiting carriers against the fee.
Expose the fake stamps
You turn away from the shakedown and lose time circling the warehouses.
Take another lane
Three self-appointed harbor watchmen block a warehouse lane and demand a protection fee from everyone carrying goods. Their ledger has official-looking stamps, but none match.
The Harbor Watch Fee
You tear up the false fee book so it cannot be reused to legitimize another shakedown.
Destroy the ledger
The carriers use the names and amounts to organize their own claims against the collectors.
Return the ledger to the carriers
A local broker pays 1,000 Berrys for the names and disappears with the book.
Sell the ledger to a broker
One watchman drops the fee ledger while leaving. Several paid carriers point to their names and ask whether the money can still be recovered.
A Worthless Receipt
You leave the pump to its protection arrangement and pay 1,000 Berrys for casks from a private seller.
Buy water elsewhere
The crew laughs, shoves you into the pump frame, and keeps the front position.
The entire quay backs the original order, leaving the pirate crew isolated without a fight.
They stop pushing forward but refuse to move their barrels.
Other crews back your demand and the cutters lose the front position.
Hold the line verbally
A barrel clips your knee and a pirate answers with a hard shove.
You clear the whole lane so quickly that the waiting dockhands close ranks behind you.
You move one barrel, but the crew blocks the rest.
You roll the barrels out of the queue before the crew can surround you.
Roll their barrels aside
A freshwater pump serves three ships before dusk. A pirate crew cuts the line with empty barrels while dockhands mutter that the pump owner pays protection to them.
The Pump Line
The ship least able to relocate takes the first load; the remaining water goes by queue order.
Serve the damaged ship first
You step away once the line is restored and let the pump owner choose who waits.
Leave the choice to the owner
Two small crews fill their casks while the largest ship waits for morning.
Serve the smaller crews first
The cutters finally step back, but the pump has lost pressure during the argument. Only two full loads can be drawn before dark.
Who Pumps First
event.active_new_world_frontier_b_01_yuk: The surface drops under one foot and you slam onto the ice before scrambling free.
You find a narrow pressure ridge that lets everyone cross without losing the sled.
You reach one surveyor but must abandon the sled as the crack opens.
You guide both surveyors over the thinnest section before it separates.
Cross light and fast
The surveyors reach stable ice while their equipment slides away with the breaking shelf.
Cut the sled loose
The rope jerks you onto the ice and the sled drops one crate into the crack.
You wrench the whole load clear just before the shelf breaks away behind it.
You move the sled only halfway before the shelf shifts again.
You drag the sled and both surveyors onto stable ice.
Haul the sled across
A blue crack races across the ice shelf beneath two surveyors and their sled. The shore is close, but the split widens with every wave under the ice.
The Shelf Cracks
The crate disappears under the shelf, but nobody risks the unstable edge again.
Cut the rope
You haul the crate up and preserve the expedition’s measurements.
Recover the instruments
The survey leader pays 1,000 Berrys for the risky recovery and gets the instruments back.
Ask for a recovery fee
Everyone reaches stable ice, but one survey crate hangs from the last rope over black water. The instruments are valuable; the shelf edge is still cracking.
One Rope Left
You keep to the mapped route and let the smoke vanish behind the ridge.
Avoid the unknown camp
You find stranded travelers burning damp driftwood and show them the safest route back.
Follow the smoke
You mark a path from the ridge so whoever made the fire can reach the main trail.
Leave route markers
A thin smoke column rises from a remote inlet where no expedition camp is marked. Snow will cover the tracks by evening, and the nearest shelter is hours away.
Smoke Beyond the Ridge
You repack the cache and raise its marker above the new snowline.
Reseal it for the team
Your navigator adds a precise bearing and date, making the cache easier to recover later.
Ask your navigator to update the marker
You treat the missing team as gone and take what the weather has not ruined.
Strip the abandoned cache
You take enough fuel to weather the coming storm and leave the food and rope intact.
Take only dry fuel
An old expedition cache emerges from melting snow: rope, dry fuel and sealed rations. The marker names a team months overdue, and a storm front is approaching.
The Half-Buried Cache
You mistake old storm stains for the normal high line and linger too long.
You identify a dry shelf that makes the entire crossing safer for the group.
You confirm the cave floods fast but cannot judge the safe window precisely.
The stain layers reveal which tunnel remains above water longest.
Read the water stains
You reject the cave and lose most of the day to the exposed headland trail.
Take the long headland route
You enter on the wrong surge and a wave throws you against the cave wall.
You read the full tide rhythm and cross with enough time to inspect a side chamber safely.
You mistime the lull and have to retreat soaked before the narrowest section.
You catch the correct lull and cross before the next surge fills the tunnel.
Time the crossing
A guide points to a sea cave that opens only between two violent tides. Inside lies a shortcut across the headland, but the waterline is already climbing.
The Tide Cave Window
You leave the old case untouched and use the shelf only to wait out the surge.
Leave it where it is
You scratch a clear tide mark for future travelers before moving on.
Mark the safe shelf
You carry the case out and later return it to the expedition camp for a small reward.
Take the map case
Halfway through, the cave opens onto a dry shelf littered with old expedition pegs and a sealed tin map case. The next surge can be heard outside.
A Dry Shelf
You mistake a wind-carved hollow for the return line and lead everyone toward a flooded inlet.
You find both the marker line and a sheltered descent the expedition missed on the way out.
You recover the general direction, but the group loses time crossing bad ground.
You match the wind to the ridge shape and recover the missing marker line.
Read wind and slope
The group shelters behind packed snow until visibility improves, losing the rest of the day.
Dig in and wait
You chase a dark shape that is only ice and expose the group to the wind.
You uncover an old expedition mark pointing to a safer route above the tide.
You find one broken cairn but cannot tell which direction it once marked.
A line of half-buried stones leads back toward the camp.
Search for old cairns
Your navigator reconstructs the return line from the wind and shore angle.
Let your navigator lead
A coastal expedition loses sight of its return markers as snow blows sideways. The tide is rising behind the group, and the camp cannot be seen from the ridge.
Markers in the Whiteout
You carve a lower but durable direction mark into the exposed rock.
Score the rocks instead
You rebuild the marker high enough to remain visible through the next snowfall.
Repair the marker
You leave the broken pole and get the expedition back across the beach before the channel fills.
Return before the tide
The return line reappears, but its final pole has snapped near a tidal channel. The group can repair it for future travelers or hurry back before the water closes the beach.
The Last Marker
